summary: Describes how S/MIME can be processed and generated by message transfer agents, guards, and gateways to deliver security services, called domain security services. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets the mailroom of a company handle locking and checking mail for everyone.

questions: how to encrypt mail between domains
subtitle: S/MIME security services at the domain boundary, not end-to-end.

tldr.problem: End-to-end S/MIME encryption and signing between different organizations is difficult due to incompatible systems, PKI barriers, and the need for message inspection at domain boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: Domain security services apply S/MIME signatures and encryption at the message transfer agent, guard, or gateway level, allowing a domain to sign and encrypt on behalf of its users.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can protect inter-domain mail without requiring desktop PKI or exposing internal systems, though this trades end-to-end security for practical organizational security.

today: RFC 3183 is an Experimental protocol from 2001. While it describes practical mechanisms for domain-level S/MIME security that address real problems in heterogeneous mail systems, it has not become an Internet Standard. Domain-level mail security remains in use in some organizations, though modern approaches often focus on gateway scanning and policy enforcement rather than S/MIME-based domain security.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Domain Security Services (DOMSEC) describes how message transfer agents, guards, and gateways can apply S/MIME encryption and signatures on behalf of an entire domain of users. The RFC addresses practical problems: heterogeneous messaging systems (some organizations use X.400, others SMTP), content screening and audit requirements that break end-to-end encryption, and the expense of deploying PKI to every employee.

Unlike end-to-end security where users sign and encrypt their own mail, domain security is applied at the organizational boundary. A domain can verify the authenticity of a message before releasing it to external recipients, or encrypt information between domains. This approach complements rather than replaces desktop security: an organization might use desktop-to-desktop signatures for internal mail but domain-level encryption for external communication.
sections.plainLanguage: A company can have its mailroom check every email and add a company signature or lock, rather than asking every employee to do it themselves. This works even if different parts of the company use different email systems.

sections.title: Domain Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC defines four domain security mechanisms built on S/MIME:

Domain Signature: A signature generated by an entity named 'domain-signing-authority' that authenticates information sent between domains or from a domain to an individual. It wraps the original message and any existing signatures, proving that the message has been reviewed and released by that domain.

Review Signature: Added by a third party (such as a mail guard) that has examined the message. A review signature indicates approval for forwarding to the final recipient, without claiming to authenticate the original sender.

Additional Attributes Signature: Applied by an 'attribute-authority' to add extra metadata to a message, such as security labels or equivalent labels defined in ESS (Enhanced Security Services).

Domain Encryption and Decryption: A 'domain-confidentiality-authority' encrypts messages on behalf of users or decrypts messages for a domain. This is useful when end users lack encryption capability or when domains use incompatible encryption schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Four ways a company can help with mail security: adding a company signature (domain signature), marking that someone checked it (review signature), adding labels (attributes), or locking/unlocking for whole groups (domain encryption).

sections.title: Message Wrapping and Signatures
sections.content:
Domain security messages use signature encapsulation: a signed or unsigned message is wrapped in a signature that covers both the content and any existing inner signatures. This ordering is important because it allows recipients to determine the order in which signatures were added. An unsigned message may first receive an empty signature layer for backward compatibility with S/MIME software that does not support DOMSEC.

Messages can be triple-wrapped: first signed by the originator, then encrypted, then signed again. A DOMSEC signature must indicate its type (originator, domain, review, or additional attributes) using a SignatureType signed attribute with a specific Object Identifier (OID). Each signature type follows naming conventions: the subject name in the certificate must be 'domain-signing-authority', 'review-authority', or 'attribute-authority', and for domain signatures, the domain part of the authority's name must match or be an ancestor of the originator's domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can be wrapped in layers like an onion. The order matters, and each layer has a label saying what type of signature it is. This way, everyone knows who checked it and in what order.

sections.title: Domain Encryption and Key Management
sections.content:
Domain encryption allows a Domain Confidentiality Authority (DCA) to encrypt messages on behalf of originators or decrypt them for recipients. The RFC describes four cases: originator encryption for end-recipient decryption (standard S/MIME), originator encryption with domain-level decryption (for content inspection), domain-level encryption for end-recipient decryption, and domain-level encryption with domain-level decryption.

The DCA is located using certificate naming conventions and name mapping rules similar to those used for signatures. When encrypting, the sending domain's DCA finds the recipient DCA's certificate in a directory (X.500, LDAP, or local store) and encrypts using that key. The RFC does not mandate a specific method for locating certificates but requires that name mapping conventions be followed to ensure confidentiality. Key material compromise for a DCA is more serious than for an individual user because it can compromise security for an entire domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A company's mailroom can lock outgoing mail using the recipient company's mailroom key, so only their mailroom can open it. They find the right key by looking up the recipient's mailroom name in a directory.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Domain security services rely on well-known names like 'domain-signing-authority' and 'domain-confidentiality-authority' that are globally visible. Organizations must take care to issue certificates with these names only to legitimate entities; a rogue certificate could allow an attacker to read messages intended for others.

Compromise of a DCA's private key is especially serious because it affects all messages encrypted for that domain. The keys used by domain authorities must be protected with great care and stored securely.

Domain encryption alone is not fully secure without a domain signature to prevent masquerade attacks. A compromised attacker with a DCA certificate could fake a message pretending to come from another domain. Additionally, if an end user's DCA decrypts a message to inspect content, that message is temporarily in plaintext and could be intercepted. If the recipient's DCA is compromised, the recipient cannot guarantee message integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: If the mailroom's security key is stolen, the attacker could read or fake all the company's messages. The mailroom keys must be locked up very carefully.
